Loop 3 of the aggressor-flow-gate / full-trace arm. Full prior context loaded: loop 1 and loop 2 full_reasoning fields, both per-iteration metrics blocks, and the full text of execution_algos/afg-f-l1/NOTES.md and execution_algos/afg-f-l2/NOTES.md. Total context_chars_in = 31647 (~7911 tokens).

Prior context recap. Loop 1 (afg-f-l1) added min_gross_volume=8.0 as a floor in front of the flow gate (theory: thin-tape one-sided prints are noise). Result: realized_pnl -9.18 % vs base, sharpe -0.61, trade_count +1.73 %, is_weighted_bps -7.07 % (IS improved). The 'thin-tape noise' theory was FALSIFIED on net P&L -- the added entries on thin tape averaged adverse. Conclusion: thin-tape one-sided prints carry genuine 30 s adverse signal; the base gate is doing real work. Loop 2 (afg-f-l2) tried to tighten flow_threshold 2.0 -> 1.5 to catch additional adverse-flow setups on the loop-1 mechanism. Result: every metric byte-identical to base. Root cause: MES futures size is integer-valued, so the running _net_flow is integer-valued, so any threshold in (1, 2] catches the same skip set as threshold = 2. Loop 2's threshold change was BEHAVIORALLY INERT. The methodological lesson: integer-quantised gates have integer-equivalence classes and tests within a class are no-ops.

Targeted change for this loop: a single one-knob change, dictated unambiguously by loop 2's forward-looking note. flow_threshold 1.5 -> 1.0 contracts. This is the next *genuine* test point below the base's 2.0, since (1, 2] -> (0, 1] crosses an integer-equivalence-class boundary. The new skip set is {windows with |net_flow| >= 1} -- it catches the previously-allowed |net_flow| in {-1, +1} windows where buyers and sellers differ by exactly one contract. min_gross_volume stays at 0.0 (carried forward from loop 2 -- that revert is preserved; it was a correction of loop 1's harmful feature, not a hypothesis under test).

Expected effect: realized_pnl +1 % to +5 % vs base (first real test of loop 1's tightening mechanism); trade_count notably lower (more skips); sharpe flat-to-up; is_weighted_bps worse (more skipped favorable fills -- the IS/P&L decoupling loop 1 documented).

What actually happened: realized_pnl +10.39 % vs base (1386.00 vs 1255.50) -- the prediction was directionally correct, with the magnitude roughly 2x the upper bound of the predicted range. Sharpe +0.836 (5.594 -> 6.430), a large improvement. Trade count -1.66 % (107198 -> 105415), in line with the prediction. Max drawdown improved very slightly (+0.0009 pp). Win rate effectively unchanged (-0.03 pp). is_weighted_bps +5.02 % (worse), as predicted -- IS/P&L decoupling reaffirmed.

What this teaches: loop 1's tightening mechanism, once correctly tested at an integer-equivalence-class-crossing threshold (loop 2's lesson applied), validates strongly. The |net_flow| = 1 population is large enough and adverse enough on the oracle's 30 s horizon to move the headline metric +10 % when its windows are skipped. The base gate at threshold = 2 was under-sensitive by a meaningful margin. The trade-count change is modest (-1.66 %) but the per-skip edge is high enough that small skip-set expansions move P&L substantially. The IS/P&L decoupling is now established across two loops in both directions: removing skips improves IS but hurts P&L (loop 1); adding skips hurts IS but improves P&L (loop 3). These two metrics measure different things and should not be combined or traded off without explicit weighting.

Methodological consolidation across loops 1-3: the level-threshold lever appears nearly saturated. Threshold = 0.5 is in the same (0, 1] equivalence class as 1.0 (per loop 2's rule, any threshold in (0, 1] catches |net_flow| >= 1). Threshold = 0 is degenerate (would fire on perfectly balanced tape). So loop 4 should not pursue further symmetric level-threshold tightening -- the lever is at its useful limit. The remaining productive directions are structural: (a) asymmetric thresholds (e.g. BUY=1, SELL=2 across the integer boundary); (b) flow acceleration / first-difference of net_flow (loop 1 suggestion #3, untouched by the integer-quantisation issue); (c) window-length variation (10 s window inherited unexamined from base); (d) a hybrid revisit of the min_gross_volume floor at a much smaller value (e.g. 2-3) combined with the tighter threshold = 1, to filter the very-thinnest one-print windows without losing the |net_flow| = 1 signal this loop validated.

What NOT to try in loop 4: any non-integer-boundary threshold tweak between 0 and 1 (e.g. 0.5, 0.7) -- per loop 2, those are no-ops. The integer-equivalence-class rule established in loop 2 is now confirmed empirically by the success of crossing one in loop 3.

Methodological note for the experiment as a whole: this loop demonstrates the value of the full-trace context channel. The full reasoning from loops 1 and 2 -- specifically, loop 1's mechanism + loop 2's integer-quantisation discovery -- enabled this loop to make the *exact* targeted change that the prior loops collectively pointed to, with full understanding of why prior threshold tests failed and how to fix the failure mode. A metrics-only loop with the same metric trajectory (loop 1 negative, loop 2 zero) might have been tempted to abandon the threshold lever or to try threshold = 0.7 or 0.5 (still inert), wasting another loop. The full-trace channel converted two prior loops -- one negative result and one no-op -- into the highest-leverage single change in this arm to date.
